verifyNote: Written from standard UK optometric practice (College CMGs, NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme, NICE). Always check against Dr Biswas's slides and the PC-lab case materials — grading and referral pathways can be local.

topics.title: History and symptoms
topics.summary: From Dr Sheppard's week 8 lecture and seminar: the history is the most important part of the eye examination (over 70% of diagnoses can come from it). Take it in a logical order, follow up every symptom with LOFTSEA, ask everyone the standard symptom check, and record negatives.
keyPoints: Ask permission to take the history; show empathy, listen actively, keep open body language and don't interrupt. Patients' uninterrupted talking time is usually 30 seconds to a minute.
General observation matters: appearance, head posture, facial asymmetry, lids, eyes, speech and emotional state; age, sex and ethnicity change the likelihood of some conditions.
Reason for visit: open with 'Is there any particular reason for your visit today?' and record it in the patient's words. Return to it at the end.

LOFTSEA: Location, Onset (sudden can mean serious), Frequency, Type and severity, Self-treatment, Effect on the patient, Associated symptoms. Visual problems tend to come with eye use, on weekdays, building through the day.
Ask everyone about distance and near vision, eyestrain, headaches, pain or burning, diplopia, and flashes and floaters (especially high myopes).
Ocular history: each pair of spectacles, contact lens wear and care, low vision aids, past injuries, infections, surgery or patching, and the last eye exam.

General health: ask specifically about high blood pressure and diabetes (how long, last check), medication (including drops, hay fever and contraceptive pills; check the BNF) and allergies or reactions to drops.
Family history: strabismus, glaucoma, hypertension and diabetes. Lifestyle: occupation, sport, hobbies, driving and smoking (the strongest environmental risk factor for AMD).
Suggested order: general information, last eye exam, reason for visit, ocular history, family ocular history, general health, family medical history, symptom check, occupation and lifestyle.
Record in pen, legibly and fully, including negatives (no record means not asked), using only accepted abbreviations.
examTraps: Accepting 'double vision' at face value: ask if they see two of everything and whether it goes with one eye closed.
Not following up a headache because the patient says it isn't their eyes.
Assuming old records are still current.

diagram.description: A funnel: wide at the top with open questions (reason for visit), narrowing through symptom details, ocular history, general health and medication, family history, and lifestyle, ending in a short list of hypotheses at the bottom.

goDeeper.heading: Symptom clues
goDeeper.body: Constant distance blur: myopia, or nuclear sclerosis in older people. Intermittent: young diabetics, pseudomyopia. Near blur fine in good light: presbyopia. Both: astigmatism or pathology. Visual headaches are mild to moderate, dull, above or behind the eyes and linked to eye use. Pain or burning often means dry eye. Diplopia that persists with one eye closed is monocular (cataract, irregular astigmatism); pathological or traumatic diplopia is more often vertical.

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: SOCRATES and red flags
goDeeper.body: For pain, SOCRATES (site, onset, character, radiation, associations, time course, exacerbating and relieving factors, severity) is another framework. Red flags include sudden vision loss, flashes with a curtain, a painful red eye, new diplopia, and headache with visual or neurological symptoms.

checklist.title: Case history structure
steps: Reason for visit / chief complaint (open question).
History of the presenting complaint: onset, duration, frequency, eye(s), severity, triggers, associations.
Ocular history: last eye exam, glasses/CLs, surgery, injuries, eye conditions.
General health: conditions (e.g. diabetes, BP), recent changes.
Family ocular history (glaucoma, AMD, squint) and medical history.
Social: occupation, driving, screens, hobbies, smoking.
Summarise back to the patient and check you've got it right.

flashcards.back: Site, onset, character, radiation, associations, time course, exacerbating/relieving, severity.
Hydroxychloroquine.

flashcards.front: Medication linked to cataract and raised IOP
flashcards.back: Corticosteroids.
Over 50, headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, sudden vision loss.
Location, Onset, Frequency, Type and severity, Self-treatment, Effect on the patient, Associated symptoms.
Linked to eye use, worse later in the day and on weekdays, mild to moderate, dull, above or behind the eyes.
Cataract and irregular astigmatism (it persists with the other eye closed).

flashcards.front: Strongest environmental risk factor for AMD
flashcards.back: Smoking.

mcq.q: A 72-year-old mentions new headaches, pain when chewing and a brief episode of vision loss in one eye. What's the priority?

options.text: Suspect giant cell arteritis — same-day referral
options.feedback: Yes — GCA can cause permanent sight loss quickly.

options.text: Routine refraction and review in a year
options.feedback: This history has red flags.
This could delay urgent treatment.
It needs same-day assessment.

mcq.explanation: Headache, jaw claudication and transient vision loss in an older person suggest GCA, a sight-threatening emergency needing urgent blood tests and steroids.

topics.askClaude: Be a patient with a hidden diagnosis. Let me take a full case history by asking you questions, then tell me what I forgot to ask.

topics.title: Building a differential diagnosis
topics.summary: A differential diagnosis is a ranked list of what could explain the findings. Rank by likelihood, but always include the conditions you can't afford to miss, then choose tests that separate them.
keyPoints: List possibilities from the key symptom and sign (e.g. 'sudden painless loss of vision in one eye').
Think anatomically (front to back) and by mechanism (vascular, inflammatory, infective, degenerative, neoplastic, traumatic).
Rank by likelihood (age, history, risk factors) and by seriousness.
Always keep 'can't miss' diagnoses on the list until ruled out (e.g. retinal detachment, GCA, angle closure).
Choose discriminating tests: pupils (RAPD), IOP, fields, staining, dilated fundus exam.
Revisit the list as new results come in.
Management follows from the most likely and most serious possibilities.
examTraps: Stopping at the first diagnosis that fits ('premature closure').
Ranking only by likelihood and forgetting serious but rarer causes.
Doing every test instead of the ones that discriminate.

diagram.description: Table-style diagram comparing red eye causes across columns: pain, photophobia, vision, discharge, pupil, cornea, IOP. Rows: conjunctivitis, subconjunctival haemorrhage, episcleritis, scleritis, anterior uveitis, keratitis, acute angle closure.

goDeeper.heading: Example: sudden painless vision loss
goDeeper.body: Differentials: retinal vein occlusion, retinal artery occlusion, vitreous haemorrhage, retinal detachment involving the macula, wet AMD, ischaemic optic neuropathy (including arteritic from GCA). Discriminators: fundus appearance, RAPD, age and systemic history, symptoms of GCA. Most need urgent or emergency referral.

goDeeper.heading: Example: gradual blur
goDeeper.body: Differentials: refractive change, cataract, dry AMD, diabetic maculopathy, glaucoma (late), medication effects. Discriminators: pinhole, refraction, lens assessment, macular exam (and OCT), fields, history (diabetes, steroids).

goDeeper.heading: Writing it down
goDeeper.body: Record the working diagnosis and the main differentials you considered, the tests that supported or excluded them, and your plan. This shows clear reasoning, which is exactly what PC-lab and OSCE-style assessments look for.

flashcards.back: A serious condition that must stay on the list until ruled out, even if less likely.
Stopping at the first diagnosis that seems to fit.

flashcards.front: Key test for optic nerve vs retinal cause of vision loss
flashcards.back: Pupils — look for a relative afferent pupil defect (RAPD).
Likely refractive cause.

mcq.q: A red eye with photophobia, ciliary flush, normal IOP and cells in the AC. Most likely?

options.feedback: Yes — cells in the AC are the key sign.
No photophobia or AC cells in simple conjunctivitis.
IOP would be very high.
No AC activity or significant photophobia.

mcq.explanation: Photophobia, ciliary flush and AC cells/flare point to anterior uveitis; it needs prompt referral.

cases.scenario: A 66-year-old with hypertension noticed sudden painless blurring in the right eye this morning. VA R 6/36, L 6/6. Fundus: widespread flame haemorrhages in all four quadrants of the right eye with dilated tortuous veins.
cases.question: What's your differential and plan?
cases.modelAnswer: Most likely central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO); differentials include hypertensive retinopathy (but it's unilateral) and diabetic retinopathy. Check BP, IOP (glaucoma is a risk factor), pupils (RAPD suggests ischaemic CRVO). Refer urgently to the hospital eye service per local guidance, and advise GP review of BP and cardiovascular risk.

topics.askClaude: Give me a presenting symptom and a few signs, ask me for a ranked differential including a 'can't miss' diagnosis, then reveal more findings one at a time.

topics.title: Diabetes and the eye
topics.summary: Diabetic retinopathy is a microvascular disease graded in England by the NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme (R0–R3, M0–M1). Diabetes also affects refraction, the lens, cranial nerves and the cornea. Know the signs in order of severity and the referral rules.
keyPoints: Earliest sign: microaneurysms. Then dot/blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots.
Pre-proliferative (R2): venous beading or reduplication, IRMA, multiple deep blot haemorrhages.
Proliferative (R3A): new vessels (on the disc or elsewhere), pre-retinal or vitreous haemorrhage, fibrosis.
Maculopathy (M1): exudate within 1 disc diameter of the fovea, a group of exudates in the macula, or haemorrhage/MA near the fovea with reduced VA.
Risk factors for progression: duration, poor glucose control (HbA1c), high blood pressure, raised lipids, pregnancy, rapid improvement in control.
Other effects: refraction shifts with blood sugar changes, earlier cataract, cranial nerve palsies (III often pupil-sparing), reduced corneal sensation, rubeosis and neovascular glaucoma.
Everyone with diabetes aged 12+ should attend annual DESP screening (intervals are being extended for some low-risk people).
examTraps: Confusing hard exudates (yellow, well-defined) with cotton wool spots (white, fluffy).
Calling cotton wool spots alone 'proliferative'.
Prescribing glasses during a period of unstable blood sugar.

diagram.description: Fundus drawing showing: microaneurysms (tiny red dots), blot haemorrhages, hard exudates (yellow, near the macula), cotton wool spots (white fluffy), venous beading, IRMA, and new vessels at the disc (NVD) and elsewhere (NVE).

goDeeper.heading: DESP grading in brief
goDeeper.body: R0 none; R1 background (MAs, haemorrhages, exudates, cotton wool spots with other non-referable features); R2 pre-proliferative (venous beading/loop/reduplication, IRMA, multiple deep round or blot haemorrhages); R3A active proliferative; R3S stable treated proliferative. M0 no maculopathy; M1 maculopathy. U = ungradable. R3A is referred urgently; R2 and M1 are referred to the hospital eye service. Check the current DESP grading definitions.

goDeeper.heading: Diabetes and refraction
goDeeper.body: High blood glucose can change the lens's refractive index and hydration, often causing a myopic shift; as control improves the refraction moves back. If someone has been recently diagnosed or their control has just changed, it's often wise to delay a new prescription until blood sugar is stable, explaining why.

goDeeper.heading: Optometrist's role
goDeeper.body: Check that patients with diabetes are attending DESP, examine the fundus (dilated where appropriate), recognise sight-threatening signs between screenings and refer accordingly, and give lifestyle messages: blood sugar, blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking, attending screening.

flashcards.back: Microaneurysms.
Active proliferative retinopathy (new vessels, pre-retinal/vitreous haemorrhage) — urgent referral.
Exudate within 1 disc diameter of the fovea.

flashcards.front: Hard exudate vs cotton wool spot
flashcards.back: Exudate: yellow, well-defined (lipid). CWS: white, fluffy (nerve fibre layer infarct).

mcq.q: A patient has venous beading and IRMA in two quadrants, but no new vessels. DESP grade?

options.feedback: Yes — venous beading and IRMA are R2 features.
R1 doesn't include venous beading or IRMA.
R3A needs new vessels or pre-retinal/vitreous haemorrhage.
M grades describe the macula.

mcq.explanation: Venous changes, IRMA and multiple deep blot haemorrhages define pre-proliferative (R2) retinopathy.

mcq.q: A newly diagnosed type 2 diabetic reports her distance vision has blurred over the last month and wants new glasses. Best advice?

options.text: Delay new glasses until blood sugar has stabilised, and explain why
options.feedback: Right — refraction can shift while control changes.

options.text: Prescribe the full new Rx today
options.feedback: It may change again within weeks.
Not without sight-threatening signs.

options.text: Tell her diabetes doesn't affect vision
options.feedback: It can affect refraction and the retina.

mcq.explanation: Fluctuating glucose changes the lens; wait for stability (and check the fundus) before finalising a prescription.

topics.askClaude: Describe 5 diabetic fundi in words and ask me to give each a DESP R and M grade and the referral action.

topics.title: Hypertension and the eye
topics.summary: High blood pressure damages retinal vessels over time (narrowing, AV nipping, wiring) and acutely in severe hypertension (haemorrhages, cotton wool spots, exudates, disc swelling). It also raises the risk of vein and artery occlusions.
keyPoints: Chronic changes: generalised and focal arteriolar narrowing, AV nipping, copper or silver wiring (arteriosclerosis).
Acute/severe changes: flame haemorrhages, cotton wool spots, hard exudates (sometimes a macular star), disc swelling.
Classifications: Keith–Wagener–Barker (grades 1–4) or the simpler Wong–Mitchell (mild, moderate, malignant).
Hypertension raises the risk of branch and central retinal vein occlusion, artery occlusion and ischaemic optic neuropathy.
NICE NG136: clinic BP of 180/120 mmHg or more with retinal haemorrhages or papilloedema needs same-day specialist assessment.
Measuring BP in practice (where trained and equipped) can support appropriate referral.
Often asymptomatic — your fundus findings may be the first clue.
examTraps: Missing bilateral disc swelling in a patient with very high BP (accelerated hypertension).
Calling AV nipping 'normal crossings'.
Forgetting to check BP and refer when you see hypertensive signs.

diagram.description: Close-up of an artery crossing over a vein. Normal crossing: vein continuous. AV nipping: vein appears narrowed/hidden either side of the artery and deflected. Copper wiring: artery with a broad orange light reflex; silver wiring: artery appears white.

goDeeper.heading: Wong–Mitchell classification
goDeeper.body: Mild: generalised or focal arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, opacity ('wiring') of arteriolar walls. Moderate: haemorrhages (blot, dot or flame), microaneurysms, cotton wool spots, hard exudates. Malignant: moderate signs plus optic disc swelling. Moderate and malignant changes carry higher cardiovascular risk.

goDeeper.heading: What to do
goDeeper.body: Mild signs: advise the patient to have their BP checked by their GP. Moderate signs: refer to the GP more promptly, ideally with a BP reading. Signs of malignant hypertension (disc swelling, widespread haemorrhages/exudates) with very high BP: same-day referral. Follow local guidance and record what you advised.

flashcards.back: Narrowing/deflection of a vein where an artery crosses it — a chronic hypertensive sign.
Radiating hard exudates around the fovea — seen in severe hypertension.
BP ≥180/120 with retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema.

flashcards.front: Eye conditions hypertension increases risk of
flashcards.back: Retinal vein and artery occlusion, ischaemic optic neuropathy.

mcq.q: A patient has bilateral disc swelling, flame haemorrhages and a macular star. BP measured in practice is 210/125. Action?

options.feedback: Yes — this is a medical emergency.
Far too slow for these findings.
It needs action today.
That's diabetic screening, not relevant here.

mcq.explanation: NICE NG136: BP ≥180/120 with papilloedema or retinal haemorrhages needs same-day specialist assessment.

topics.askClaude: Help me tell diabetic and hypertensive retinopathy apart. Describe mixed fundi and ask me which signs belong to which, and what I'd do.

topics.title: Interpreting clinical data in PC-lab cases
topics.summary: PC-lab cases give you a patient's history and a set of results to interpret. Work systematically: check the data makes sense, compare eyes and visits, decide what's abnormal, link the findings into a diagnosis, then decide management.
keyPoints: Read the whole case first; note age, symptoms, history and risk factors.
Check consistency: does the VA fit the refraction? Did pinhole improve it?
Compare right with left and today with previous visits — change and asymmetry are often the key.
Know your normal ranges (IOP, C/D, amplitude, fusional reserves, NIBUT).
Visual fields: check reliability first, then pattern (arcuate, altitudinal, hemianopic, quadrantic, central).
Bitemporal defects suggest chiasmal lesions; homonymous defects suggest lesions behind the chiasm.
Finish with a clear diagnosis, differentials, management and urgency.
examTraps: Interpreting an unreliable field as real.
Ignoring the 'boring' data (e.g. pinhole VA) that explains the case.
Giving a diagnosis without management and urgency.

diagram.description: Visual pathway from eyes through optic nerves, chiasm, optic tracts, LGN and radiations to occipital cortex, with lesion sites numbered. Beside each, the matching field defect: 1 optic nerve → monocular loss; 2 chiasm → bitemporal hemianopia; 3 optic tract → homonymous hemianopia; 4 temporal radiation → superior quadrantanopia; 5 parietal → inferior quadrantanopia; 6 occipital → homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

goDeeper.heading: Visual field reliability
goDeeper.body: Before reading any defect, look at fixation losses, false positives and false negatives. High false positives (trigger-happy patient) make fields look better than they are; high false negatives can mimic defects. Commonly used cut-offs (e.g. false positives above about 15% with SITA) mark a test as unreliable — check the values your module uses. Repeat unreliable fields.

goDeeper.heading: Field indices
goDeeper.body: Mean deviation (MD): overall depression compared with age-matched normals (more negative = worse). Pattern standard deviation (PSD): how irregular the loss is (higher = more localised defects). Glaucoma hemifield test (GHT) compares superior and inferior field: 'outside normal limits' is suspicious. Look at the pattern deviation plot to see localised loss beyond general depression (e.g. cataract).

goDeeper.heading: Structuring your answer
goDeeper.body: 1) Summary of the key abnormal findings. 2) Most likely diagnosis and why. 3) Differentials and what rules them out. 4) Management: what you'd do, who you'd refer to and how urgently. 5) What you'd tell the patient. This structure works for almost every case.

flashcards.back: Optic chiasm.
Behind the chiasm (tract, radiations or occipital cortex).
MD = overall depression; PSD = irregularity/localised loss.

flashcards.front: First thing to check on a visual field
flashcards.back: Reliability indices.

mcq.q: A field shows a right superior quadrantanopia in both eyes, matching closely. Most likely lesion site?

options.feedback: Yes — 'pie in the sky', contralateral temporal lesion.
Chiasm gives bitemporal defects.
That affects one eye only.
Parietal lesions give inferior quadrantanopias on the opposite side.

mcq.explanation: Inferior fibres loop through the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop) and carry the superior field; a left-sided lesion affects the right field.

mcq.q: A field has 30% false positives and shows an 'excellent' result. How should you treat it?

options.feedback: Right — high false positives make fields look falsely good.
It can't be trusted.
There's no evidence of that from this test.
Always check reliability first.

mcq.explanation: False positives (pressing without a stimulus) inflate sensitivity, hiding real defects.

cases.scenario: A 45-year-old reports bumping into things on both sides. VA 6/6 each eye. Fields show bitemporal hemianopia respecting the vertical midline. Discs show slight temporal pallor.
cases.question: What's the likely cause and urgency?
cases.modelAnswer: A chiasmal lesion, most commonly a pituitary adenoma. Refer urgently (same week or as local guidance for suspected neurological causes; same day if there are acute symptoms like sudden severe headache or vision loss) for neuroimaging and investigation. Explain the need for further tests without speculating on tumours.

topics.askClaude: Give me a PC-lab style case with VA, refraction, IOP, disc and field results. Let me interpret it step by step, then mark my answer.

topics.title: Referral urgency and writing referrals
topics.summary: Choosing the right urgency and writing a clear referral gets the patient seen by the right person at the right time. The College of Optometrists' Clinical Management Guidelines give urgency for most conditions; follow local pathways for where to send it.
keyPoints: Urgency categories (College CMGs) include emergency (same day), urgent (within about a week) and routine — check the exact definitions you're taught.
Emergency examples: retinal detachment, acute angle closure, suspected GCA, microbial keratitis, chemical injury (irrigate first), papilloedema.
Urgent examples: suspected wet AMD (via fast-track pathway), anterior uveitis (often same/next day), new unexplained field defects.
Routine examples: cataract affecting lifestyle, suspected COAG/OHT, stable chronic conditions.
Where to: eye casualty, hospital eye service via the local pathway, GP, or community schemes — depends on the condition and local services.
Referral letter contents: patient details, reason and urgency, history, relevant findings with numbers (VA, IOP, fields), what you've told the patient, your details and signature.
Tell the patient why, how urgently, and what to do if things get worse; record the referral.
examTraps: Under-calling urgency for GCA or retinal detachment.
Writing vague letters ('?glaucoma, please see').
Not telling the patient what to expect or what to do if symptoms worsen.

diagram.description: Three columns: Emergency (same day) — RD, acute angle closure, GCA, MK, chemical injury, papilloedema. Urgent — wet AMD fast-track, anterior uveitis, new field loss. Routine — cataract, COAG suspect, stable conditions.

goDeeper.heading: A good referral letter
goDeeper.body: Dear Doctor / Colleague, Re: [name, DOB, address, NHS number if known]. Reason: e.g. 'Suspected COAG left eye — routine.' History: symptoms, relevant medical history and medication. Findings: VA, IOP with method and time, disc description/C/D, fields (with printout), other relevant results. Action taken and advice given. Your name, GOC number, practice details, date, signature. Keep it factual and concise.

goDeeper.heading: GOS 18 and local pathways
goDeeper.body: In England, the GOS 18 form is used to refer NHS patients from a sight test; many areas now use electronic referral systems and community schemes (e.g. glaucoma repeat measures, cataract direct referral, minor eye conditions services). Know your local pathway — and as a student, always involve your supervisor.

goDeeper.heading: Safety-netting
goDeeper.body: Tell the patient what to watch for and what to do if it happens: 'If you notice a curtain coming over your vision, more flashes or a shower of floaters, go to eye casualty straight away.' Write down what you told them.

flashcards.back: RD, acute angle closure, suspected GCA, microbial keratitis, chemical injury, papilloedema.
Urgent via the fast-track pathway.

flashcards.front: England NHS referral form from a sight test
flashcards.back: GOS 18 (or the local electronic equivalent).
Telling the patient what symptoms to watch for and what to do if they happen.

mcq.q: A 58-year-old has new flashes, a shower of floaters and a shadow in the upper field of the right eye. Urgency?

options.feedback: Yes — suspected retinal detachment.
A shadow suggests detachment — far too slow.
RD can progress to involve the macula quickly.
Not safe.

mcq.explanation: Flashes + floaters + a field shadow = suspected RD; same-day referral to eye casualty.

mcq.q: Which line belongs in a referral letter?

options.text: 'IOP R 26, L 18 mmHg (Goldmann, 10:30); L disc C/D 0.4, R 0.65 with inferior thinning.'
options.feedback: Specific, measurable and relevant.
Too vague to act on.
Diagnosis is for the specialist; describe findings.
The key findings should be in the letter.

mcq.explanation: Good referrals give precise findings with method, time and comparison between eyes.

topics.askClaude: Give me 6 short scenarios and ask me the referral urgency and destination for each, then help me write one full referral letter.

topics.title: The non-traumatic red eye
topics.summary: Sorting a red eye by history and a few signs: one eye or both, pain, photophobia, vision, discharge, pupil, cornea and anterior chamber. From the week 3 tutorial tables.
keyPoints: Unilateral red eye: think infection, acute glaucoma or iritis. Bilateral: conjunctivitis is more likely.
Conjunctivitis: viral is watery with cold symptoms and follicles; allergic is watery and itchy with puffy lids and papillae; bacterial is mucoid and crusty with lids stuck together.
Papillae: raised, red, central vessel, on the palpebral conjunctiva (allergy, bacteria, contact lenses). Follicles: pale domes with vessels around them, lower fornix (viral).

Corneal ulcer: pain, photophobia, watering and reduced VA with staining and an infiltrate. Contact lens wear and smoking point to infection; systemic illness such as rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis or inflammatory bowel disease points to a non-infectious cause.
Episcleritis: mild pain, VA normal, vessels move over the sclera. Scleritis: moderate to severe pain, VA reduced, vessels do not move, with intraocular inflammation.
Endophthalmitis: sudden painful red eye with cells, flare and hypopyon.
examTraps: Not noticing what the record leaves out: questions that weren't asked and tests that weren't done.
Giving one referral urgency for a condition whose urgency depends on the findings.
Mixing up papillae and follicles: follicles go with viral infection.

goDeeper.heading: Pupil clues
goDeeper.body: A distorted pupil suggests iritis. An oval, mid-dilated pupil suggests angle closure. Photophobia also points towards iritis or acute angle closure.

goDeeper.heading: Marginal keratitis and recurrent erosion
goDeeper.body: In the tutorial table, marginal keratitis has no pain or photophobia and normal VA, with staining and a stromal infiltrate. Recurrent corneal erosion gives pain and photophobia with staining but no infiltrate.

flashcards.front: Discharge in viral, allergic and bacterial conjunctivitis
flashcards.back: Viral: watery (can become mucoid). Allergic: watery. Bacterial: mucoid, crusty.

flashcards.front: Episcleritis or scleritis: which has vessels that move over the sclera?
flashcards.back: Episcleritis.

flashcards.front: Systemic conditions linked to non-infectious corneal ulcers
flashcards.back: Ankylosing spondylitis, inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis.

flashcards.front: Treatment of allergic conjunctivitis in the tutorial table
flashcards.back: Antihistamine eye drops and avoiding the allergen.

mcq.q: A red eye with mild pain, normal VA, a clear cornea and anterior chamber, and vessels that move over the sclera is most likely

options.feedback: Yes: mild pain, normal VA, mobile vessels and a quiet eye.
Scleritis gives moderate to severe pain, reduced VA and vessels that don't move.
That is sudden and painful, with cells, flare and hypopyon.
The cornea would stain and show an infiltrate, with reduced VA.

mcq.explanation: From the episcleritis, scleritis and endophthalmitis comparison table.

mcq.q: Follicles in the lower fornix with watery discharge and recent cold symptoms suggest

options.feedback: Yes: follicles, watery discharge and cold symptoms or fever.
Allergic gives itching, puffy lids and papillae.
Bacterial gives mucoid, crusty discharge with lids sticking.
That is a cause of papillae, not follicles.

mcq.explanation: From the conjunctivitis and papillae-versus-follicle tables.

cases.scenario: A contact lens wearer who smokes has a painful, photophobic, watering red eye with reduced VA. The cornea stains and shows an epithelial opacity with a stromal infiltrate.
cases.question: Which type of corneal ulcer does this fit, and which features point you there?
cases.modelAnswer: An infectious corneal ulcer. Contact lens wear and smoking are the risk factors in the tutorial table, with no systemic illness; pain, photophobia, watering, reduced VA, and staining with an epithelial opacity and stromal infiltrate complete the picture. A non-infectious ulcer would more typically have no lens wear and a systemic illness such as rheumatoid arthritis.

topics.askClaude: Explain The non-traumatic red eye to me step by step, then quiz me on it.

topics.title: Lids and orbit: lagophthalmos and proptosis
topics.summary: Incomplete lid closure and a bulging eye, from the week 4 tutorials: the causes to tell apart, the tests that matter, and how urgent each one is.
keyPoints: For lagophthalmos the needed tests are history, VA, cover test, motility and external examination; pupils, refraction, internal examination and IOP aren't needed.
Ectropion: urgent (2 weeks) if the cornea stains; routine if the cornea is normal.
Myasthenia gravis: intermittent binocular diplopia that varies with gaze, fatigable ptosis worse on sustained upgaze, lagophthalmos and surface staining.

Carotid-cavernous fistula: abnormal artery-to-cavernous-sinus connection (trauma or spontaneous, e.g. Ehlers-Danlos). Bruit, pulsating proptosis, brick-red vessels, chemosis, cranial nerve palsies; can cause angle-closure glaucoma or optic neuropathy.

Orbital cellulitis: infection spreading from sinuses, teeth or ears; sudden unilateral proptosis, lid oedema and redness, painful restricted movement, diplopia, RAPD. Can spread to the brain or cavernous sinus.
Thyroid eye disease: expansion of orbital fat and connective tissue, lid retraction, lagophthalmos, proptosis and incomitant deviation; red, staining eye when active, white when chronic.
examTraps: Forgetting that pinhole failing to improve VA rules out uncorrected refractive error.
Giving one urgency for conditions whose urgency depends on findings (ectropion, orbital tumour, TED).

goDeeper.heading: Why a fistula affects so much
goDeeper.body: High-pressure arterial blood enters the cavernous sinus and pushes back through the superior ophthalmic vein, so orbital veins become dilated and tortuous (chemosis, proptosis). The swollen sinus also presses on cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI as they pass through.

goDeeper.heading: Orbital tumour urgency
goDeeper.body: In the tutorial table: urgent within 1 week if there is blurred vision, limited movement, pain, red eye or corneal staining with ptosis, lagophthalmos and proptosis; routine if VA, comfort and the ocular surface are normal.

flashcards.front: Sign you might hear in carotid-cavernous fistula
flashcards.back: A bruit (a whooshing sound).
Fatigable ptosis, worse on sustained upgaze.

flashcards.front: Where does orbital cellulitis usually spread from?
flashcards.back: Sinuses, teeth or ears.

flashcards.front: Cranial nerves at risk in the cavernous sinus
flashcards.back: III, IV, V1, V2 and VI.

mcq.q: Sudden bulging of one eye with painful limited movement, lid oedema and redness, and an RAPD most suggests

options.feedback: Yes: sudden unilateral proptosis with painful restriction and optic nerve involvement.
Chronic TED is usually bilateral, slower and white.
Ectropion is a turned-out lid, not proptosis.
A routine tumour has normal VA and no pain.

topics.askClaude: Explain Lids and orbit: lagophthalmos and proptosis to me step by step, then quiz me on it.

topics.title: Diplopia
topics.summary: Working out the cause of double vision from the case record: which muscles and nerves are involved, how each cause looks, and which need urgent action. From the week 6 tutorial.
keyPoints: SO4 LR6 (rest)3: superior oblique is supplied by IV, lateral rectus by VI, all other extraocular muscles by III.
Sixth nerve palsy: sudden horizontal diplopia worse in the affected direction, esotropia, limited abduction.
Fourth nerve palsy: vertical or oblique diplopia, hypertropia, head tilted towards the opposite shoulder.
Third nerve palsy: oblique diplopia, exotropia and hypotropia, limited adduction, elevation and depression, possibly ptosis and a poorly reacting dilated pupil.
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: poor adduction of one eye with nystagmus of the abducting eye; linked to multiple sclerosis.
Decompensated phoria: intermittent diplopia worse when tired; the cover test shows poor recovery or breakdown to a tropia; everything else normal.
In the tutorial, palsies and gaze palsy come with swollen discs, which changes urgency and whether dilation is safe.
examTraps: Missing that diplopia varies with gaze direction: that points to a palsy, not a decompensated phoria.
Dilating without thinking about whether it's safe in a patient with a possible neurological problem.

goDeeper.heading: Gaze palsy
goDeeper.body: Sudden horizontal diplopia with limited movement of both eyes towards one side, unusual headaches and neurological symptoms, with swollen discs: think of an intracranial cause such as an aneurysm, and refer as an emergency.

flashcards.back: Superior oblique: IV (trochlear). Lateral rectus: VI (abducens). Everything else: III (oculomotor).

flashcards.front: Head posture in a fourth nerve palsy
flashcards.back: Tilted towards the opposite shoulder.
Poor adduction on the affected side with nystagmus of the abducting eye; often multiple sclerosis.

mcq.q: Sudden horizontal diplopia, worse on looking to the left, with a left esotropia and limited left abduction suggests

options.feedback: Yes: the lateral rectus (VI) abducts the eye.
That gives vertical diplopia and hypertropia.
That gives exotropia with limited adduction, elevation and depression.
That is intermittent and doesn't limit movement.

mcq.explanation: From the tutorial's sixth nerve palsy profile and the SO4 LR6 rule.

topics.askClaude: Explain Diplopia to me step by step, then quiz me on it.

topics.title: Headache and pain in or around the eye
topics.summary: Most headaches aren't visual, but eye pain or headache can signal angle closure, iritis, orbital disease or a neurological problem. From the week 8 tutorials and the history and symptoms lecture.
keyPoints: Follow up any headache with LOFTSEA, even if the patient thinks it isn't visual.
Visual headaches are linked to eye use, mild to moderate, dull and above or behind the eyes; only a small proportion of headaches are visual.
Pupil clues in eye pain: distorted in iritis; oval and mid-dilated in acute angle closure.
Painful proptosis suggests orbital cellulitis or an orbital tumour.
Headache types met in the tutorial include chronic daily headache (CDH) and episodic tension-type headache (ETTH).
examTraps: Assuming a headache is visual because the patient needs glasses: look for features that don't fit and for neurological signs.
Skipping tests the case needs, such as pupils and IOP, in a patient with eye pain.

flashcards.back: Oval and mid-dilated, poorly reacting.
Small or distorted (posterior synechiae).
Chronic daily headache; episodic tension-type headache.

mcq.q: A patient with a painful red eye has an oval, mid-dilated pupil. Which is most likely?

options.feedback: Yes.
Iritis gives a small or distorted pupil.
The pupil is normal.
The pupil is normal.

topics.askClaude: Explain Headache and pain in or around the eye to me step by step, then quiz me on it.

topics.title: Visual field loss: causes and urgency
topics.summary: When a patient reports losing part of their vision, the history, IOP, fundus and field pattern separate retinal, optic nerve and brain causes, and set the urgency. From the week 9 tutorial.
keyPoints: Retinal detachment: vision lost like a curtain, IOP under 10 mmHg, tobacco dust (Shafer's sign), pale elevated retina. Macula-on vs macula-off changes urgency.
Acute optic neuropathy: sudden blur and unusual headaches with a hyperaemic, swollen disc. Progressive forms are gradual, with a swollen or a pale disc.
Wet AMD: sudden one-eyed blur with drusen, haemorrhage, grey-green membrane, exudates and oedema. Dry AMD: routine referral for low vision help if the patient wants it.
Glaucoma: gradual, painless, repeatable field loss that respects the horizontal midline.
Brain disease: transient bilateral blur, headaches worse lying down, flashes, neurological symptoms, swollen discs, and homonymous loss respecting the vertical midline.
TIA: seconds of blur or sparkling lights with neurological symptoms (vertigo, weakness, numbness); everything else normal.
examTraps: Missing low IOP as a clue to retinal detachment.
Giving a single urgency for conditions where it depends on the findings (e.g. macula on or off, how recent wet AMD is).

flashcards.back: Pigment ('tobacco dust') in the anterior vitreous, suggesting a retinal tear or detachment.

flashcards.front: Field loss respecting the vertical midline
flashcards.back: Points to the chiasm or behind it (brain), not the retina or optic nerve.

flashcards.front: Headache worse lying down plus swollen discs
flashcards.back: Raised intracranial pressure: an emergency.

mcq.q: A patient describes a curtain over their vision. IOP is 8 mmHg in that eye and there's pigment in the anterior vitreous. Most likely?

options.feedback: Yes: curtain, low IOP and Shafer's sign.
Glaucoma is gradual, often with raised IOP.
Lasts seconds, and the eye is normal.
Gradual central loss.
